questions.scenario: A team runs a nightly ETL job on Amazon ECS. The job takes 25 minutes. Management wants to eliminate all server patching. A developer proposes migrating the job to AWS Lambda to reduce cost. What is the correct assessment?
options: Lambda is suitable because 25 minutes is within its limits
Lambda is unsuitable because the job exceeds the 15-minute maximum timeout; ECS on Fargate removes patching instead
Lambda is suitable if memory is set to 10,240 MB
Lambda is suitable if the job is split across 25 sequential invocations of one minute each
questions.explain: Lambda's hard maximum is 15 minutes, so a 25-minute job cannot run in a single invocation regardless of memory. Switching the ECS launch type to Fargate achieves the actual goal — no servers to patch — without redesigning the job. Option 4 sounds plausible but would require inventing checkpointing and orchestration that does not exist in the scenario.

questions.scenario: A DynamoDB table has partition key tenant_id. One tenant generates 90 percent of traffic and that tenant's requests are throttled while overall table capacity is barely used. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Increase provisioned capacity on the table
Add a suffix to the partition key to shard that tenant's items across multiple partitions
Switch the reads to eventually consistent
Add a global secondary index on tenant_id
questions.explain: Capacity is distributed across partitions, so a single hot partition throttles even when the table has spare capacity overall. Write sharding — appending a calculated suffix such as tenant_id#3 — spreads that tenant across partitions. Adding capacity does not help because the ceiling is per-partition. Eventually consistent reads halve read cost but do not fix write concentration, and a GSI on the same key reproduces the same skew.

questions.scenario: An application publishes to an SNS topic with two SQS queues subscribed. One queue's consumer has been offline for six hours. What happens to messages published during that time?
options: They are lost because SNS could not deliver them
They remain in that SQS queue until the consumer returns, subject to the retention period
They are automatically routed to the other queue
SNS retries only for one hour then discards them
questions.explain: SNS delivers to the SQS queue, not to the consumer, so delivery succeeded the moment the message entered the queue. Messages then wait in the queue for up to the retention period (4 days by default, 14 maximum) until the consumer returns. This is precisely why SQS is placed between SNS and consumers rather than subscribing consumers directly.

questions.scenario: A Lambda function has reserved concurrency set to 5. During a traffic spike, invocations are throttled. A developer sets provisioned concurrency to 5 as well. What is the effect on throttling?
options: Throttling stops because provisioned concurrency adds capacity
Throttling continues because reserved concurrency still caps the function at 5 concurrent executions
Throttling stops because provisioned concurrency overrides reserved concurrency
The function can now scale to 1,000
questions.explain: Reserved concurrency is a hard ceiling on simultaneous executions — provisioned concurrency does not raise it. Provisioned concurrency only pre-warms environments within that ceiling, removing cold starts but not increasing capacity. To stop throttling, the reserved concurrency limit itself must be raised or removed.

questions.scenario: An application must process messages exactly once and in order. Which TWO configurations are required?
options: Use an SQS FIFO queue
Set a MessageGroupId on each message
Enable long polling
Set a visibility timeout of 12 hours
Use a standard queue with content-based deduplication
questions.explain: Only FIFO queues provide exactly-once processing and ordering, and ordering is guaranteed within a message group, so a MessageGroupId is required. Long polling reduces empty receives without affecting semantics, a long visibility timeout only delays redelivery, and standard queues do not support deduplication at all.

questions.scenario: An API Gateway REST API integrates with a Lambda function that takes 20 seconds. Users report intermittent 504 errors under load, though the function logs show completion in 20 seconds every time. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: The function occasionally exceeds the 29-second API Gateway integration timeout when cold starts are added
The Lambda timeout is set to 20 seconds
API Gateway caching is misconfigured
The function returns an invalid response shape
questions.explain: A 20-second execution leaves only 9 seconds of headroom before the fixed 29-second API Gateway integration timeout. Under load, cold start initialisation added to execution time can exceed it, producing intermittent 504s while the function itself still records a normal 20-second duration. An invalid response shape would produce 502 rather than 504.

questions.scenario: A developer stores a 500 KB JSON document as a single DynamoDB item and receives a validation error. What is the correct remedy?
options: Enable DynamoDB compression
Store the document in S3 and keep the S3 key plus metadata in DynamoDB
Split the document across 2 items of 250 KB each
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity
questions.explain: DynamoDB items cannot exceed 400 KB and this limit cannot be raised. The standard pattern stores the large payload in S3 and keeps only a pointer and queryable attributes in DynamoDB. Splitting across items forces the application to reassemble and loses atomicity, DynamoDB has no built-in item compression feature, and capacity is unrelated to size limits.

questions.scenario: An SQS consumer processes a message successfully but crashes before calling DeleteMessage. What happens?
options: The message is deleted automatically after processing
The message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and is processed a second time
The message is moved to the dead-letter queue immediately
The message is lost
questions.explain: SQS deletes a message only when DeleteMessage is called explicitly. If the consumer crashes first, the visibility timeout expires and the message returns to the queue for reprocessing. This is why consumers must be idempotent — SQS standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once.

questions.scenario: A Lambda function was attached to a VPC to reach an RDS instance. It now fails when calling the Amazon SNS API. What is the cause and the MOST cost-effective fix?
options: Lambda lost internet access in the VPC; add an interface VPC endpoint for SNS
The execution role lost permissions; reattach the policy
SNS does not support VPC access; move the call to a second function outside the VPC
The function needs more memory; increase the allocation
questions.explain: A VPC-attached Lambda function loses default internet access, so calls to public AWS API endpoints fail. An interface VPC endpoint for SNS routes the traffic privately and is cheaper than running a NAT gateway. Nothing in the scenario changed IAM permissions, and the failure began with the VPC attachment rather than memory.

questions.scenario: An application uses DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda consumer. Processing fails repeatedly for one record and the entire shard stops progressing. Which setting prevents one bad record from blocking the stream?
options: Configure BisectBatchOnFunctionError and MaximumRetryAttempts with an on-failure destination
Increase the Lambda timeout
Increase the stream retention period
Enable provisioned concurrency
questions.explain: Stream consumers process records in order per shard, so a persistently failing record blocks everything behind it — the poison pill problem. BisectBatchOnFunctionError narrows the batch to isolate the offending record, and MaximumRetryAttempts with an on-failure destination discards it to a queue for investigation so the shard advances. Timeouts, retention and concurrency do not unblock the shard.

questions.scenario: Which statement about Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon SQS is correct?
options: Both allow multiple independent consumers to read the same message
Kinesis retains records for re-reading by multiple consumers; SQS deletes a message once consumed
SQS retains records for 365 days
Kinesis guarantees exactly-once delivery by default
questions.explain: Kinesis records persist for the retention period and each consumer tracks its own position, so many consumers can read the same records and replay them. In SQS a message is consumed and deleted by one consumer. SQS maximum retention is 14 days, and Kinesis provides at-least-once delivery, so consumers must handle duplicates.

questions.scenario: A developer wants a Lambda function to reuse a database connection across invocations, but connections are occasionally dropped by the database. What is the correct implementation?
options: Create the connection outside the handler and validate or recreate it inside the handler if unhealthy
Create a new connection inside the handler every time
Store the connection object in an environment variable
Store the connection in a Lambda layer
questions.explain: Initialising outside the handler enables reuse across warm invocations, but because environments live for a long time and connections can be dropped, the handler must check health and reconnect when necessary. Creating a connection every invocation wastes latency. Environment variables hold only strings, and layers ship read-only code.

questions.scenario: An application must guarantee that a DynamoDB write and an SQS message send either both happen or neither does. Which approach is MOST reliable?
options: Write to DynamoDB, then send the message, and hope both succeed
Write to DynamoDB and use DynamoDB Streams to trigger the message send
Send the message first, then write to DynamoDB
Use TransactWriteItems across DynamoDB and SQS
questions.explain: DynamoDB transactions cannot span other services, so no cross-service transaction exists. The transactional outbox pattern solves this: commit the write to DynamoDB, then let Streams reliably trigger the downstream send from the committed change, so the message is sent only if the write succeeded. Doing the two operations independently in either order can leave them inconsistent when one fails.

questions.scenario: Which combination BEST supports a request that must return within 100 ms while performing work that takes 5 seconds?
options: Increase the API Gateway timeout to 5 seconds
Accept the request, enqueue the work, return 202 Accepted with a status URL
Run the work in a synchronous Lambda with more memory
Cache the response in API Gateway
questions.explain: When required latency is far below the work duration, the work must become asynchronous: accept and validate the request, enqueue it, return 202 immediately with a way to check status, and process in the background. Extending timeouts still makes the client wait 5 seconds, more memory cannot compress genuinely long work into 100 ms, and caching cannot serve a result that does not exist yet.

questions.scenario: A developer notices that a DynamoDB Query with a FilterExpression returns few items but consumes capacity as though many were read. Why?
options: Filters are applied after items are read, so capacity is consumed for every item matching the key condition
The table is under-provisioned
The filter syntax is invalid
Filters always trigger a full table scan
questions.explain: A FilterExpression runs after DynamoDB reads the items matching the key condition, so read capacity reflects everything read, not what is returned. Reducing cost requires a better key design or an index, not a filter. A Query is still bounded by the key condition, so it does not scan the entire table.

questions.scenario: An application must ensure that S3 objects uploaded by users are processed exactly once, but S3 event notifications can occasionally be delivered more than once. What should the processing function do?
options: Track processed object keys and version IDs in DynamoDB and skip duplicates
Rely on S3 to deduplicate events
Set the Lambda timeout very low
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
questions.explain: S3 event notifications guarantee at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible and the consumer must be idempotent — recording processed keys and version IDs makes reprocessing a no-op. S3 does not deduplicate notifications, and neither timeout settings nor Transfer Acceleration affect delivery semantics.

questions.scenario: Which approach reduces the risk of exceeding the 1,000 default concurrent execution limit when several functions share an account?
options: Set reserved concurrency on non-critical functions to cap their share
Increase every function's memory
Enable provisioned concurrency on all functions
Disable CloudWatch logging
questions.explain: Reserved concurrency caps how much of the account pool a given function may consume, guaranteeing headroom for critical functions. Memory does not affect concurrency limits, provisioned concurrency reserves capacity from the same pool and can make contention worse, and logging settings are unrelated.

questions.scenario: A Step Functions Standard workflow must call a Lambda function that occasionally fails with a transient error. What is the recommended configuration?
options: A Retry block with exponential backoff on the task state, plus a Catch for terminal failures
A Wait state before the task
Increasing the Lambda memory
Using an Express workflow instead
questions.explain: Step Functions task states support declarative Retry blocks with configurable interval, backoff rate and maximum attempts, along with Catch blocks to route terminal failures — no orchestration code required. A Wait state merely delays, memory does not address transient errors, and Express workflows change execution semantics and duration limits rather than retry behaviour.

questions.scenario: Which statement about Lambda function versions is correct?
options: A published version is immutable, including its code and configuration
Versions can be edited after publishing
Versions share environment variables with $LATEST dynamically
Only one version can exist per function
questions.explain: Publishing a version freezes the code and configuration, including environment variables, which is what makes aliases and traffic shifting safe. $LATEST remains mutable for ongoing development, versions do not track later changes to it, and a function may have many versions.

questions.scenario: An application must fan out an event to 10 downstream consumers, each with different filtering needs, and consumers are added frequently. Which design scales BEST operationally?
options: EventBridge with one rule per consumer and content-based filtering
Ten direct API calls from the producer
One SQS queue polled by all consumers
A Lambda function that calls each consumer in a loop
questions.explain: EventBridge lets each consumer own a rule with its own filter pattern, so adding or changing a consumer never touches producer code. Direct calls and loop-based dispatch couple the producer to every consumer and fail together. A single shared SQS queue delivers each message to only one consumer.

questions.scenario: A developer must choose between DAX and ElastiCache to reduce DynamoDB read latency, and the deciding requirement is minimal application code change. Which is correct and why?
options: ElastiCache, because it supports more data structures
DAX, because it is API-compatible with DynamoDB so typically only the client endpoint changes
ElastiCache, because it is cheaper in all cases
DAX, because it supports Redis commands
questions.explain: DAX exposes the DynamoDB API, so an application usually only points its client at the DAX endpoint and gains write-through caching automatically. ElastiCache requires explicit cache-aside logic for reads, writes and invalidation. Richer data structures are a Redis advantage but irrelevant here, and DAX does not speak Redis commands.

questions.scenario: A developer adds an S3 bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject to a role. The role's identity policy has an explicit Deny for s3:GetObject on that bucket. What is the result?
options: Access is granted because the bucket policy allows it
Access is denied because an explicit deny in any policy overrides all allows
Access depends on which policy is evaluated first
Access is granted only from the VPC
questions.explain: An explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluation — identity policy, resource policy, SCP or permission boundary — always wins. The order in which policies are evaluated never matters because deny takes precedence unconditionally.

questions.scenario: An application encrypts 10 MB files by calling kms:GenerateDataKey once per file, then discards the plaintext data key. To reduce KMS API costs for millions of small files, what is the recommended optimisation?
options: Reuse a cached plaintext data key for multiple files within a bounded scope and lifetime
Call kms:Encrypt directly on each file
Disable encryption for small files
Store the plaintext data key in the object metadata
questions.explain: Caching a data key and reusing it for a bounded number of objects within a limited time reduces KMS calls substantially — the pattern the AWS Encryption SDK implements with configurable limits. Calling kms:Encrypt directly fails above 4 KB, disabling encryption breaks the requirement, and storing the plaintext key alongside the ciphertext destroys the protection entirely.

questions.scenario: A Lambda function must access a secret. A developer places the secret in an environment variable encrypted with the default AWS managed key. A reviewer objects. What is the valid concern?
options: Environment variables cannot be encrypted at all
Anyone with GetFunctionConfiguration permission can read the decrypted value in the console or API
The 4 KB limit prevents storing any secret
Encrypted environment variables slow down cold starts significantly
questions.explain: With the default AWS managed key, Lambda decrypts environment variables transparently, so any principal able to view the function configuration sees the plaintext. Using a customer managed key with encryption helpers keeps the value ciphertext until the function decrypts it at runtime. Variables are encrypted at rest by default, and the 4 KB limit accommodates typical secrets.

questions.scenario: An application in Account A assumes a role in Account B. The AssumeRole call fails with AccessDenied. Which TWO-part configuration must be verified?
options: The role's trust policy in Account B names the Account A principal, and Account A's identity policy allows sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN
Only the trust policy in Account B
Only the identity policy in Account A
The role must be in the same region as the caller
questions.explain: Cross-account role assumption requires both sides to agree: Account B's trust policy must name the calling principal, and Account A's identity policy must permit sts:AssumeRole on that role ARN. Either alone yields AccessDenied. IAM is a global service, so region is irrelevant.

questions.scenario: Which TWO statements about Amazon Cognito are correct?
options: A user pool issues JWTs after authenticating a user
An identity pool exchanges a token for temporary AWS credentials
A user pool issues AWS access keys directly
An identity pool stores usernames and passwords
A user pool can only be used with mobile applications
questions.explain: User pools are user directories that authenticate and return ID, access and refresh tokens as JWTs. Identity pools take a trusted token and return temporary AWS credentials via STS so the client can call AWS services. User pools never issue AWS credentials directly, identity pools do not store user records, and user pools serve web, mobile and server applications alike.

questions.scenario: An organisation requires that no developer can create an IAM role with permissions broader than a defined set, even if they have IAM write access. Which feature enforces this?
options: A permission boundary attached to the roles they create, enforced by a condition in their own policy
An S3 bucket policy
A KMS key policy
A CloudWatch alarm
questions.explain: Permission boundaries cap the maximum effective permissions of a principal, and requiring via a condition that any role a developer creates must carry a specified boundary prevents privilege escalation. Bucket and key policies govern specific resources, and alarms only detect after the fact.

questions.scenario: A presigned S3 URL generated by a Lambda function stops working after one hour, even though the expiration was set to 24 hours. Why?
options: Presigned URLs cannot exceed one hour
The temporary credentials used to sign the URL expired after one hour, invalidating it
S3 revoked the URL
The object storage class changed
questions.explain: A presigned URL is only valid while the credentials that signed it remain valid. A Lambda execution role's temporary credentials typically last about an hour, so the URL dies with them regardless of the requested expiry. Longer-lived URLs require signing with credentials that last at least as long. Storage class does not affect URL validity.

questions.scenario: Which approach correctly restricts an API Gateway REST API so it can only be invoked from within a VPC?
options: Create a private API endpoint with an interface VPC endpoint and a resource policy allowing that endpoint
Use a regional endpoint with an API key
Use an edge-optimized endpoint with a Lambda authorizer
Place the API in a private subnet
questions.explain: A private API endpoint is reachable only through an interface VPC endpoint, and its resource policy restricts access to that endpoint ID. API keys identify callers without restricting network origin, authorizers authenticate rather than isolate, and API Gateway is a managed service that is not deployed into your subnets.

questions.scenario: A security team requires that a KMS key used for a compliance workload cannot be deleted for at least 30 days after a deletion request. What must be configured?
options: Nothing — KMS enforces a mandatory waiting period of 7 to 30 days, and 30 is the default
A CloudWatch alarm on deletion events
An S3 lifecycle rule
A key policy denying all Decrypt actions
questions.explain: KMS never deletes keys immediately; scheduling deletion begins a mandatory waiting period between 7 and 30 days, with 30 as the default, during which the deletion can be cancelled. Alarms provide notification but no enforcement, lifecycle rules apply to S3 objects, and denying Decrypt would break the workload without preventing deletion.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST appropriate way to grant a third-party monitoring tool read-only access to CloudWatch metrics in your account?
options: Create a role with a trust policy for the vendor's account including an external ID, granting read-only CloudWatch permissions
Create an IAM user and email the access keys
Share your root account credentials
Make the metrics public
questions.explain: A cross-account role with an external ID lets the vendor assume it for temporary, least-privilege credentials, and the external ID protects against the confused deputy problem. Emailing access keys creates a long-lived credential outside your control, root credentials must never be shared, and CloudWatch metrics cannot be made public.

questions.scenario: An application writes logs containing session tokens. A developer proposes encrypting the log group with KMS to resolve the finding. Is this sufficient?
options: Yes, encryption fully resolves the exposure
No — anyone authorised to read the logs still sees the tokens; the tokens must not be logged at all
Yes, provided a customer managed key is used
No, but shortening retention to one day resolves it
questions.explain: Encryption at rest protects against access to the underlying storage, not against authorised log readers, who would still see the tokens in plaintext. The correct fix is to redact or omit sensitive values before they are written. Shortening retention narrows the exposure window but leaves the tokens readable while they exist.

questions.scenario: Which statement about SSE-KMS versus SSE-S3 for an audited workload is correct?
options: SSE-KMS logs each key use in CloudTrail and allows key policy control; SSE-S3 does not
SSE-S3 provides a CloudTrail audit trail of key usage
Both provide identical auditing
Neither can be audited
questions.explain: SSE-KMS uses a KMS key whose every encrypt and decrypt operation is recorded in CloudTrail and whose access is governed by a key policy — exactly what an audit requirement needs. SSE-S3 uses keys managed entirely by S3 with no per-use audit trail or customer-controlled policy.

questions.scenario: A developer must ensure an IAM policy applies only when the caller has authenticated with MFA within the current session. Which condition should be used?
options: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to true
aws:SecureTransport set to true
aws:PrincipalArn matching a wildcard
aws:RequestedRegion
questions.explain: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true only when the requesting credentials were obtained with MFA, which is the standard way to gate sensitive actions. aws:SecureTransport enforces TLS, PrincipalArn matches identity, and RequestedRegion constrains geography — none of which relate to MFA.

questions.scenario: An S3 bucket must be readable only through a specific CloudFront distribution and not directly. What should be configured?
options: Origin Access Control on the distribution with a bucket policy allowing only that distribution
A public bucket with a CloudFront distribution in front
An IAM user for CloudFront
S3 Transfer Acceleration
questions.explain: Origin Access Control lets CloudFront sign requests to S3, and a bucket policy permitting only that distribution's service principal blocks direct access to object URLs. Leaving the bucket public means the origin URLs still work and bypass CloudFront entirely. CloudFront does not use IAM users, and Transfer Acceleration is unrelated to access control.

questions.scenario: Which practice correctly implements least privilege for a CI/CD pipeline role that deploys CloudFormation stacks?
options: Grant the role only the CloudFormation and target-service actions needed, scoped to the specific stacks and resources
Grant AdministratorAccess so deployments never fail
Grant iam:* so the pipeline can create any role
Use the root account for deployments
questions.explain: Scoping the pipeline role to the specific CloudFormation operations and the resource types it genuinely manages limits the blast radius of a compromised pipeline. AdministratorAccess or blanket IAM permissions turn a pipeline compromise into a full account compromise, and root credentials must never be used for automation.

questions.scenario: A developer must verify that an S3 object was not modified after upload. Which mechanism supports this?
options: Compare the stored checksum (for example SHA-256) with a recomputed checksum on download
Check the object's last modified date only
Rely on the bucket policy
Enable Transfer Acceleration
questions.explain: S3 supports additional checksum algorithms recorded with the object, so recomputing and comparing on retrieval detects any modification. A last modified timestamp shows when a change occurred but not whether the content matches the original, bucket policies control access rather than integrity, and Transfer Acceleration affects network path only.

questions.scenario: Which statement about AWS managed keys versus customer managed keys in KMS is correct?
options: Customer managed keys support custom key policies, rotation control and cross-account grants; AWS managed keys do not
AWS managed keys can be shared across accounts
AWS managed keys allow custom key policies
Both types can be deleted immediately
questions.explain: Customer managed keys give full control: key policies, grants, rotation settings and cross-account access. AWS managed keys are created and controlled by the service, cannot have custom policies or be shared across accounts, and neither key type can be deleted immediately because a waiting period always applies.

questions.scenario: A CloudFormation update changes an RDS instance's DBInstanceIdentifier. A change set shows Replacement: True. What is the consequence of executing it?
options: The property updates in place with no data impact
A new database instance is created and the original is deleted, which can lose data unless a snapshot or retention policy protects it
The stack update is rejected automatically
Only the identifier changes
questions.explain: Replacement: True means CloudFormation creates a new resource and deletes the old one, so an RDS instance would be recreated empty and the original removed. This is exactly why change sets are reviewed before execution and why stateful resources carry DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy settings such as Retain or Snapshot.

questions.scenario: A developer adds a new environment variable to a Lambda function through the console, but the change disappears after the next pipeline deployment. Why?
options: Lambda does not support environment variables
The infrastructure-as-code template is the source of truth and overwrites manual console changes on deploy
Environment variables expire after 24 hours
The variable exceeded the 4 KB limit
questions.explain: When resources are managed by CloudFormation or SAM, each deployment reconciles the live configuration back to the template, discarding manual drift. The variable must be added to the template so the change is versioned and durable. Environment variables do not expire, and a single small variable would not exceed 4 KB.

questions.scenario: Which deployment approach allows the fastest rollback for a Lambda function that has just shifted 100 percent of traffic to a new version?
options: Repoint the alias to the previous version
Redeploy the previous code from source and wait for the build
Delete the function and recreate it
Restore the function from a snapshot
questions.explain: Because the previous version still exists and is immutable, repointing the alias reverts traffic almost instantly with no build or deployment. Rebuilding from source takes minutes, deleting and recreating causes an outage and loses configuration, and Lambda has no snapshot restore mechanism.

questions.scenario: A buildspec.yml runs tests in the build phase and the tests fail, but the pipeline continues to the deploy stage. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The test command's non-zero exit code is being suppressed, for example by piping or a trailing || true
CodeBuild ignores test results by design
The deploy stage runs in parallel with build
buildspec.yml cannot run tests
questions.explain: CodeBuild fails a phase when a command returns a non-zero exit code, so a pipeline that proceeds despite failing tests usually has that status masked by piping into another command or an explicit || true. CodeBuild does honour exit codes, stages run sequentially, and buildspec files routinely run tests.

questions.scenario: Which statement about SAM's Globals section is correct?
options: It sets default properties such as runtime, timeout and memory for all functions, which individual resources can override
It defines global variables accessible in function code
It applies to all stacks in the account
It replaces the Resources section
questions.explain: Globals declares shared defaults for common properties across serverless resources in a template, reducing repetition, and any individual resource may override them. It is template-level rather than account-level, does not inject runtime variables into code, and never replaces Resources.

questions.scenario: An ECS service update replaces tasks but users experience brief connection errors. Which setting MOST directly addresses this?
options: Configure a load balancer deregistration delay and container health checks so connections drain before task termination
Increase the task CPU
Reduce the desired count to 1
Disable the load balancer
questions.explain: Connection errors during deployment usually mean tasks are terminated while still serving requests. A deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish before the target is removed, and health checks ensure replacements are ready before traffic shifts. CPU sizing does not affect draining, reducing capacity worsens availability, and removing the load balancer eliminates the routing layer entirely.

questions.scenario: Which TWO statements about CloudFormation nested stacks are correct?
options: They allow reuse of common templates across multiple parent stacks
Updating a nested stack is done by updating the parent stack
Nested stacks can be deleted independently of the parent
Nested stacks bypass the resource limits entirely with no structure
Nested stacks require StackSets
questions.explain: Nested stacks package reusable template components referenced by a parent, and the parent stack manages their lifecycle, so updates flow through the parent. Deleting a nested stack directly breaks the parent's state, they help organise large templates rather than removing limits arbitrarily, and StackSets are a separate multi-account and multi-region feature.

questions.scenario: A team wants deployments to production to pause automatically if the error rate rises during the rollout. Which combination achieves this?
options: A canary or linear CodeDeploy configuration with CloudWatch alarms configured for automatic rollback
A manual approval action only
A larger instance type
Deploying at night
questions.explain: Gradual traffic shifting combined with CloudWatch alarms lets CodeDeploy detect elevated errors during the rollout and roll back automatically before most users are affected. Manual approvals gate the start but do not monitor the rollout, and instance sizing and deployment timing do not detect regressions.

questions.scenario: Which is true about the artifacts section of a buildspec.yml?
options: It declares which files CodeBuild passes to the next pipeline stage
It installs dependencies
It defines the container image
It sets environment variables
questions.explain: The artifacts section lists the files and directories CodeBuild uploads as output for downstream stages. Dependencies are installed in the install phase, the build image is set in the project configuration or the image field, and environment variables are declared in the env section.

questions.scenario: A stack deployment fails with 'Resource limit exceeded'. What is the MOST appropriate first action?
options: Check the relevant service quota and request an increase, or reduce the resources created
Delete all other stacks
Switch regions permanently
Disable rollback
questions.explain: That error indicates an account or region service quota has been reached, so the fix is to inspect the specific quota in Service Quotas and either request an increase or reduce consumption. Deleting unrelated stacks is destructive, switching regions avoids rather than solves the issue, and disabling rollback leaves failed stacks in a partial state.

questions.scenario: Which approach ensures that a container image deployed to production is exactly the one that passed testing?
options: Promote the same immutable image digest through environments rather than rebuilding per environment
Rebuild the image for each environment from the same Dockerfile
Use the latest tag in every environment
Build the image on the production host
questions.explain: Promoting a specific digest guarantees byte-identical artifacts across environments, so what was tested is what runs. Rebuilding can produce different images because dependencies and base layers change over time, the latest tag is mutable, and building on production introduces variance and risk.

questions.scenario: Which statement about API Gateway stage deployment is correct?
options: Changes to an API are not live until a deployment is created and associated with a stage
Changes take effect immediately on save
Each stage requires a separate API
Stages cannot have different variables
questions.explain: API Gateway separates configuration from release: edits are staged until you create a deployment and associate it with a stage, which is what makes multiple environments from one API definition possible. Stages belong to one API and each can define its own stage variables.

questions.scenario: A developer wants to run the same SAM application in two AWS accounts with different configuration. What is the recommended approach?
options: One template with parameters, deployed per account with different parameter values
Two divergent templates maintained separately
Hard-code account IDs in the template
Manually create resources in the second account
questions.explain: Parameterising environment-specific values keeps a single reviewed template as the source of truth while allowing per-account differences at deploy time. Divergent templates drift, hard-coded account IDs prevent reuse, and manual creation loses reproducibility entirely.

questions.scenario: Which happens when CodeDeploy's AfterAllowTraffic hook returns a failure for a Lambda deployment?
options: The deployment rolls back and the alias returns to the previous version
The deployment completes anyway
The function is deleted
The alias is removed
questions.explain: A failing lifecycle hook marks the deployment as failed, and CodeDeploy shifts traffic back by repointing the alias to the previous version. This is why AfterAllowTraffic is the natural place for automated post-deployment validation. The function and alias are never deleted.

questions.scenario: Which practice reduces the risk that a long-running CloudFormation update leaves resources inconsistent?
options: Break large templates into smaller stacks with clear boundaries and use change sets
Put every resource in one very large template
Disable rollback for faster failures
Update resources manually in the console
questions.explain: Smaller, well-bounded stacks limit the blast radius of any single failed update and make change sets easier to review meaningfully. One enormous template makes every change risky, disabling rollback leaves partial state behind, and manual console changes create drift that later deployments overwrite.

questions.scenario: An application's average latency is 80 ms but users complain about slowness. The p99 is 4 seconds. What does this indicate?
options: A small fraction of requests are very slow, which averages conceal
The average is wrong
All requests are slow
The metric period is too long
questions.explain: A large gap between the average and the p99 means most requests are fast while a minority are dramatically slower — often caused by cold starts, cache misses, retries or a hot partition. Because users experience individual requests rather than averages, tail latency drives complaints, which is why percentiles are the right measure.

questions.scenario: A Lambda function's Duration metric is stable but its Throttles metric is rising. What should the developer investigate FIRST?
options: Whether concurrency limits, reserved concurrency or the account limit are constraining scaling
Whether the function has a memory leak
Whether the deployment package is too large
Whether logging is disabled
questions.explain: Throttles count invocation requests rejected because a concurrency limit was reached, so the limit — reserved on the function or the account-wide pool — is the immediate suspect. Duration is unaffected, which rules out slower execution. Memory behaviour, package size and logging do not cause throttling.

questions.scenario: An X-Ray service map shows a red node for DynamoDB with a high fault rate, while the Lambda node appears healthy. What does this indicate?
options: Calls to DynamoDB are failing, and the function is likely surfacing or absorbing those errors
The Lambda function has a bug in its handler code only
DynamoDB is unavailable globally
Tracing is misconfigured
questions.explain: A red downstream node means the subsegments for those calls recorded faults — commonly throttling, conditional check failures or permission errors — so investigation should start with the DynamoDB error responses. A global outage would affect far more than one node, and a misconfigured trace would show missing data rather than specific faults.

questions.scenario: Which change is MOST likely to reduce cost for a Lambda function that is consistently CPU-bound and runs for 10 seconds at 512 MB?
options: Increase memory so more CPU is allocated, reducing duration enough to offset the higher per-millisecond rate
Decrease memory to 128 MB
Increase the timeout to 15 minutes
Add more layers
questions.explain: Lambda allocates CPU proportionally to memory, so a CPU-bound function often finishes disproportionately faster at higher memory, and because billing is memory multiplied by duration the total can fall. Reducing memory makes CPU-bound work slower and frequently more expensive, while timeouts and layers do not affect execution speed.

questions.scenario: A CloudWatch alarm on a custom metric shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA most of the time. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The metric is published sporadically, so some evaluation periods contain no datapoints
The alarm threshold is too high
The metric namespace is invalid
The alarm has no SNS action
questions.explain: INSUFFICIENT_DATA means the evaluation period contained no datapoints, which is typical for sparse custom metrics. Remedies include publishing a zero value when nothing happens or configuring how missing data is treated. Threshold values, namespaces and notification actions do not produce this state.

questions.scenario: An application shows increasing memory usage in Lambda over successive warm invocations until it fails. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: State accumulating in the global scope across invocations, such as an unbounded cache or growing array
Insufficient ephemeral storage
Too few layers
An expired IAM role
questions.explain: Because execution environments persist, data appended to module-level variables on each invocation is never released and grows until the function exhausts memory. Caches in global scope need bounds and eviction. Ephemeral storage is separate disk space, layers are read-only code, and IAM roles refresh automatically.

questions.scenario: Which metric combination BEST indicates that an SQS-triggered Lambda is keeping up with load?
options: ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage staying low while ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible remains stable
Invocations increasing only
Duration decreasing only
NumberOfEmptyReceives increasing
questions.explain: A consistently low oldest-message age with a stable visible-message count shows consumers are draining the queue as fast as producers fill it. Rising invocations alone could accompany a growing backlog, falling duration says nothing about queue depth, and empty receives simply indicate polling an idle queue.

questions.scenario: A developer must reduce API Gateway costs for an endpoint receiving many identical GET requests for data that changes hourly. Which change is MOST effective?
options: Enable stage caching with a TTL close to one hour
Increase the Lambda memory
Add more stages
Enable X-Ray tracing
questions.explain: Caching identical GET responses for close to the data's change interval eliminates most backend invocations, cutting both Lambda and downstream cost. Memory affects execution speed rather than request volume, extra stages add no caching, and tracing adds observability cost without reducing traffic.

questions.scenario: An application intermittently receives 429 TooManyRequests from API Gateway. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Requests are exceeding the configured throttling rate or burst limit and should be retried with backoff
The Lambda function crashed
The IAM role lacks permissions
The payload is too large
questions.explain: 429 indicates throttling at the API Gateway layer, either from the account or stage rate and burst limits or from a usage plan quota. The client should back off and retry, and the limits may need raising. A crashed function yields 502, missing permissions yield 403, and oversized payloads yield 413.

questions.scenario: Which approach gives the MOST accurate picture of end-user experience for a web application?
options: Real user monitoring combined with synthetic canaries from multiple locations
Only server-side latency metrics
Only CPU utilisation
Only log volume
questions.explain: Real user monitoring captures what actual users experience including network and rendering time, while synthetic canaries provide consistent baseline probes from chosen locations and detect outages even without traffic. Server-side latency omits everything beyond the load balancer, and CPU and log volume are infrastructure signals rather than experience measures.

questions.scenario: A team notices that CloudWatch Logs costs have grown far faster than traffic. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: Verbose debug logging left enabled in production and no retention policy; reduce log level and set retention
The log group name is too long
Too few metric filters
The region is wrong
questions.explain: Ingestion and indefinite retention are the two drivers of CloudWatch Logs cost, and debug-level logging left on in production inflates both. Lowering the log level and setting a retention period addresses each. Log group naming, metric filter counts and region choice do not explain disproportionate growth.

questions.scenario: An application calls three independent AWS services sequentially, each taking 200 ms, giving 600 ms total. Which change reduces latency MOST?
options: Issue the three calls concurrently so total latency approaches 200 ms
Increase the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
Add a retry to each call
Enable X-Ray tracing
questions.explain: Independent calls have no ordering requirement, so running them concurrently means total time approaches the slowest single call rather than their sum. Raising the timeout only permits longer execution, retries add latency when they trigger, and tracing measures latency without reducing it.
